part_title: API Gateway Routing and Security, AppConfig and Step Functions

scenes.title: Direct API Gateway to AWS service
scenes.narration: This diagram shows API Gateway sending data straight to Kinesis without placing a Lambda function between them. Follow the path from the client. The client posts an event to the slash events API. API Gateway maps the incoming JSON into the format required by Kinesis PutRecord. The gateway then assumes the configured IAM role and calls the specific Kinesis data stream. After Kinesis accepts the record, a response mapping transforms its service response into something simpler for the caller, such as a result saying accepted. The event can later be consumed by a Kinesis consumer and written to S3. Look at the lower request-mapping panel: the application fields such as user ID, action and timestamp become a Kinesis Data payload, accompanied by a partition key. The role panel shows that permission must be limited to the intended stream and PutRecord action. The response mapping is also important. Accepted means Kinesis received the event; it doesn't mean every downstream consumer finished processing. Compare this with Lambda integration: if we need extra validation or custom business logic, Lambda might be justified. But simply forwarding well-structured events can often use a direct AWS service integration.

scenes.title: Choose an API Gateway REST endpoint type
scenes.narration: Here the slide compares three REST API endpoint types, each serving a different network path. In the left panel, an edge-optimised endpoint uses an API Gateway-managed CloudFront distribution to help clients in widely distributed locations reach the API. In the centre, a regional endpoint exposes an API in a selected AWS Region. Internet clients can reach it, and a team can optionally place its own CloudFront distribution in front when needed. On the right, a private REST API is reached through an interface VPC endpoint and controlled by a resource policy. The diagram also shows permitted paths from other VPCs or on-premises networks using suitable private connectivity. Notice the difference between regional location and private access: a regional API is not automatically private merely because it runs in one Region. Think of a global public mobile application, a regional backend, and an internal corporate service. They may require different endpoint choices. Endpoint type determines where traffic enters; authentication and backend authorisation are separate concerns. Choose based on the caller's location, the required network exposure, and supported API type rather than memorising one endpoint as universally better.

scenes.title: Protect an AI API
scenes.narration: This slide layers several controls around an AI endpoint. Start on the left with two kinds of callers: an AWS service caller using signed IAM requests, and an end user carrying an identity token. At the API Gateway entry point, authentication and authorisation decide whether the request can continue. AWS WAF can block certain malicious request patterns where supported, while usage plans and throttling help control request volume. The backend then invokes the AI service or application using least-privilege permissions. Now read the three example results below the main architecture. A request with missing or invalid credentials receives an unauthorised response. A valid request within limits can receive the model output. An otherwise authenticated client that exceeds its quota or throttle can receive a too-many-requests response. This distinction matters: proving identity is different from deciding permissions, and both are different from limiting usage. An API key or usage plan is not sufficient user authentication. For a Bedrock-backed service, these layers protect both sensitive data and expensive inference capacity. The bottom boxes reinforce the responsibilities: authentication identifies, authorisation restricts actions, throttling manages demand, and backend IAM limits the blast radius.

scenes.title: API Gateway fronting generative AI
scenes.narration: Let's trace a complete generative AI request. A web app, mobile app or business user sends a prompt through API Gateway. The gateway applies the configured authentication method, quotas, rate limits and monitoring before forwarding to Lambda. Lambda can validate the prompt, enrich it with authorised context, apply safety controls and call Bedrock. Bedrock returns generated content and usage information. Lambda formats the application response for the caller. Notice the feedback branch in the diagram: users may also provide ratings and comments that are stored alongside minimal, appropriately handled request metadata. This can help evaluate the feature over time, but sensitive prompts shouldn't be logged indiscriminately. The lower section highlights cost and capacity controls and two request patterns. For a quick inference, the client can wait synchronously for a result within the API timeout. For a longer job, an asynchronous pattern should return a job identifier and deliver the outcome later. A model's response time isn't controlled simply by increasing API throttling. The core idea is that API Gateway protects and exposes the entry point while Lambda and Bedrock do different kinds of work behind it.

scenes.title: Control models with AppConfig
scenes.narration: This architecture illustrates changing model selection without redeploying application code. Follow the numbered route across the top. A user request reaches the application, which retrieves or uses cached AppConfig configuration. That configuration contains a primary model identifier, a fallback model identifier and a token limit. The application chooses the model according to those settings, then calls Bedrock. In the diagram, model A is the primary path and model B is the fallback if the primary isn't available under the application's rules. AppConfig stores and deploys configuration; it doesn't itself invoke the model or guarantee that a fallback is authorised. Now look at the lower rollout and rollback illustrations. A configuration update can be deployed gradually, perhaps to ten percent of targets, then fifty percent, and finally all targets, while health indicators are monitored. If the configuration causes problems, the previous values can be restored. The panel distinguishes switching the model reference from deploying a new model. An application can point to a different existing Bedrock model without rebuilding its code, but it must still validate the model ID, permissions, parameter compatibility and cost.

scenes.title: Use AppConfig feature flags for AI
scenes.narration: This slide turns model experimentation into a controlled rollout. Two request paths are shown: the stable baseline and a candidate path with a different prompt, model or settings. AppConfig supplies a feature flag that routes a gradually increasing share of requests to the candidate, from ten percent to fifty percent and then, if the results are good, to a full rollout. But why not switch everyone at once? Look at the monitoring column. Safety metrics must stay under their harmful-content threshold. Quality must meet or exceed the baseline. Cost per request must stay within the allowed budget. If a threshold is breached, the design returns traffic to the baseline configuration. This is more than a simple toggle: it is a reversible experiment with measurable success criteria. Imagine a customer-support summariser and a marketing-email writer. They may respond very differently to the new model, so the test population and metrics must match the actual use case. AppConfig helps distribute configuration; application code implements the routing and the team defines meaningful monitoring and rollback conditions.

scenes.title: Orchestrate a GenAI workflow with Step Functions
scenes.narration: This slide follows a multi-stage generative AI workflow across the screen. Begin with Validate input, where the workflow checks the user request and parameters. Next, Retrieve context gathers relevant documents or conversation history. Invoke model sends that prepared context to a model. Evaluate outcome checks the response against quality and safety rules, and Persist response saves the approved result or its metadata. Under each stage, the slide shows what comes in and what should go out. This is a crucial distinction: each task should pass only the information that the following task actually needs. The dotted error path and Catch branch show how the workflow can handle invalid input or a failed operation instead of silently stopping. The bottom compares Standard and Express workflows. Standard is appropriate when a durable, auditable execution history and longer-running coordination matter. Express is optimised for high-volume, shorter event-driven work, with different execution characteristics. Step Functions coordinates the stages; it does not replace the model, retrieval service or data store. Think of it as the visible control flow that makes a multi-service AI system easier to troubleshoot and recover.

scenes.title: Step Functions state types
scenes.narration: Here we have a visual reference to the building blocks of a Step Functions state machine. Start with Task: it actually performs work, such as calling Bedrock for a summary or invoking Lambda. Choice examines data and selects a branch, which could route an unsafe response to review instead of delivery. Parallel starts independent branches that can run concurrently, such as separate model checks that are combined afterward. In the next row, Map applies a repeated set of steps to each item in a collection; imagine processing many documents individually. Wait pauses a workflow for a scheduled interval, perhaps before a retry. Pass forwards or reshapes data without calling an external worker. Finally, Succeed and Fail explicitly end an execution with the corresponding outcome. The illustrations explain why these types are distinct: a Choice isn't a loop, and a Parallel branch isn't the same as iterating through a document list. A resilient AI workflow often combines several of these states, with controlled retries and error handlers. The exam skill is to match the state type to the operation visible in the requirement, rather than treating the state machine as one giant Lambda function.
